text:
Johnson does not rest the case on his own admiration, which might be the admiration of one age and one temper. He asks what time has done to the work. A writer whose fame depends on the fashion of his day, on local customs or on the quarrels of a party, may be praised while that fashion lasts; but the fashion passes, and the praise passes with it. Only works that continue to please readers who share none of the circumstances of their first audience can be said to have proved their worth, for such readers bring no partiality to the trial. They have no friendship with the author and no stake in his opinions, and they read him only because he still gives pleasure.

By this measure Shakespeare had already been tried. He had outlived his rivals and his patrons, and a century and a half of shifting taste, of new manners and new rules of writing, had gone over him without lessening the delight he gave. Johnson records the result in a single image (Johnson 1765): "The stream of time, which is continually washing the dissoluble fabricks of other poets, passes without injury by the adamant of Shakespeare."
